claims.claim: The impersonation rollout decision cannot be implemented as designed: the platform sync call decided impersonation goes behind a per-project flag, but RFC-001 explicitly specifies the feature 'can be enabled/disabled only at the system level' via applicationcontroller.enable.impersonation in argocd-cm, applicable to all Applications once flipped. Either the RFC's system-level flag design must be reworked or the per-project rollout decision cannot hold; no document assigns an owner to reconcile them.

The roadmap and the PRD make incompatible commitments about ApplicationSet deletion: the strategy document states deletion of generated Applications is 'explicitly out of scope' and that 'ordered or automated deletion of ApplicationSet children will not be implemented,' with teardown remaining a manual one-at-a-time operator action, while the PRD's stated goal is shipping exactly that ordered automated deletion via the deletionOrder field (AllAtOnce/Reverse). Note-2 records that someone spotted this disagreement but explicitly did not decide it and it still has no owner.

The PRD's Reverse deletionOrder is scheduled into the exact failure mode the incident review restricted against: T-28511 reproduced a delete/recreate infinite loop with reverse deletion order (the wait for full deletion never completes on a stuck Progressing app and the wave restarts), and note-2's standing runbook rule is to switch ApplicationSets to AllAtOnce before any manual child deletion until the controller fix lands. The PRD nonetheless records 'No immediate Risks to consider' and note-1 moves the dev pair onto this deletion loop now, so a workstream is being staffed into behavior the incident runbook currently forbids in operation.

T-26271's mystery is already solved in note-1 but the ticket does not reflect it: the reporter blames the broad cluster Secret credential for CI 'argocd app diff' permission failures, while the platform sync call root-caused it as impersonation making the diff run as the destination service account that lacks patch on cluster-scoped resources. The action item to note the root cause on the ticket ('so the reporter stops chasing the cluster secret') is recorded only in the meeting note, so the reporter is still chasing the wrong mechanism.

The hydrator pilot on T-27949's repository violates the incident review's interim restriction: note-2 rules that hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until a debounce exists (each hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave), yet T-27949 describes actively piloting the source hydrator on a RollingSync ApplicationSet repository where every hydration commit is picked up as a source change. The restriction was supposed to be carried onto the pilot ticket and is not there, so the pilot team is running exactly the forbidden combination.

Promoting Progressive Sync to Stable (T-28927) is scheduled as if the feature's known execution defects were closed, but two open bugs contradict the Stable definition it cites ('tested and validated, considered mature'): T-27949's RollingSync spec-only change gap leaves children OutOfSync while the rollout reports complete, and T-28511's delete/recreate loop is mitigated only by a manual runbook rule per note-2. Nothing in the promotion ticket names either as a gate, so Stable could ship with an active incident-mitigation runbook still in force.

The push-to-stage mode's cross-team dependency is unowned: T-26443's stale-manifest auto-sync occurs precisely because 'the external promoter has not yet moved the fresh manifests to the deployment branch,' RFC-002 designs push-to-stage to rely on 'some external system' for promotion while declaring a promotion system a non-goal, and note-1 records that the stage-branch promoter is still an unowned shell script that got parked. Every push-to-stage workstream therefore depends on a component nobody owns.

T-24578 and the PRD are the same underlying demand (ordered deletion of ApplicationSet-generated Applications) pursued in two uncoordinated designs that never cite each other: T-24578 wants DAG-based Application destroy ordering via a Source Hydrator for ApplicationSets, while the PRD delivers deletion ordering via the deletionOrder field on the RollingSync strategy. Whichever ships first changes whether the other is still needed, and both sit under the strategy document's explicit exclusion of automated ApplicationSet child deletion.

Note-1's deprioritization of hydrator rollback to next quarter collides with the impersonation rollout gate in the same note: per-project impersonation enablement is blocked 'until the diff story is fixed,' and T-28695 shows the diff story is not just T-26271's CLI path but the application-controller reconcile path on external clusters ignoring destinationServiceAccounts entirely (the App rotating Synced/Unknown). No ticket or note assigns the diff-path impersonation fix to anyone, so the condition gating the impersonation rollout has no owning workstream while staff moves to the deletion loop.

T-27327's proposed rollback mechanism (commit old rendered manifests directly to the sync branch, bypassing the staging branch) will collide with T-28239's signing enforcement if both land: the commit server signs hydrated commits and the operator enforces SourceIntegrity on the hydrated branch with fail-fast 'refuses to push any commit it cannot locally verify,' while the rollback flow is a plain git checkout/commit/push to that same enforced branch. Neither ticket mentions the other, and note-1's deprioritization of T-27327 makes it likely signing ships first and silently breaks the later rollback design.

T-26271's CI diff failures and the platform-sync notes describe the same root cause without the ticket saying so: with the sync impersonation flag enabled, `argocd app diff` runs as the destination service account, which lacks the RBAC to server-side-apply cluster-scoped resources. The notes record the root cause and observe the reporter is still 'chasing the cluster secret' because nobody wrote it onto the ticket — the audit trail of the incident diverges from the tracker of record.

RFC-001 commits that impersonation 'can be enabled/disabled only at the system level' (the `application.sync.impersonation.enabled` key in `argocd-cm`, applicable to all Applications once flipped), while the platform sync decided rollout 'goes behind a per-project flag, not fleet-wide' — and T-26271 already reports projects that 'recently enabled the sync impersonation flag' individually. The decided rollout control does not exist in the design being shipped; either the spec's system-level-only goal or the rollout decision must give.

The strategy document states that ordered or automated deletion of ApplicationSet children 'will not be implemented' and 'teardown remains a manual operator action, performed one Application at a time,' while the PRD ships exactly that as `deletionOrder: Reverse` inside `ApplicationSetStrategy`. The incident-review note flags the disagreement and records that it has no owner, so the organization currently holds two contradictory commitments about who or what performs deletions.

T-28695 shows the impersonation model splitting identity per operation: sync honors `destinationServiceAccounts`, but Server-Side Diff still runs as the standing cluster Secret credential. To keep diffs working, operators have added five rounds of real `patch` grants to the deliberately least-privilege cluster credential — because Kubernetes RBAC has no dry-run verb, each grant is genuine write authority guarded only by Argo CD's convention of sending `dryRun=All`. RFC-001's stated security goal (shrink the control-plane credential's attack surface) is being reversed in practice by the very feature meant to achieve it, and the Kubernetes audit trail now records two different identities acting for the same Application.

RFC-001's Example 3 explicitly relies on the `argocd-manager` service account with a `cluster-admin` ClusterRoleBinding, created by `argocd cluster add`, while impersonation narrows only the sync identity. The RFC's privilege-escalation mitigation governs who may configure `defaultServiceAccount`, but the standing cluster-admin credential is quietly kept in the cluster Secret — the same credential T-28695 shows still being used, and widened, for the diff path. An auditor verifying least privilege after impersonation ships would find the old broad credential intact and actively exercised.

T-9095 (an open request that Argo CD respect users' existing Kubernetes RBAC instead of duplicated Argo-specific RBAC) and RFC-001 (which moves sync authorization onto Kubernetes-native RBAC via impersonated ServiceAccounts) converge on the same access model without citing each other. The governance consequence: RFC-001 advances T-9095's ask for the sync path only — the acting identity becomes the destination ServiceAccount, recorded in the Kubernetes audit trail (which RFC-001 confirms captures both actual and impersonated user) — while UI/API actions like pod deletion still run under Argo's own RBAC, so access review must now cover two parallel authorization systems for the same users.

RFC-002 introduces a standing `repository-write` secret (GitHub App private key) for the hydrator's commit server, and T-28239 records that every commit that credential pushes is unsigned — if signature verification is enabled on the hydrated branch, Argo CD rejects its own output, so verification stays off. The combination means any holder of the write credential can push manifests indistinguishable from legitimate hydrator output onto the branch Argo CD deploys from, with no cryptographic evidence an auditor could use to distinguish hydrator commits from credential misuse until T-28239's signing feature ships.

RFC-002's push-to-stage mode exists so that 'Argo CD relies on some external system to move changes to the deployment branch' — the promotion gate is the control point on what reaches production. T-27327 proposes that rollback 'directly updates the sync branch (bypassing the staging branch)' in both modes. These cannot both hold as controls: a rollback becomes a write to the deployment branch that no promotion system reviewed, performed by the same hydrator/commit-server credential, leaving the change history the promoter audits incomplete for exactly the highest-risk operations.

T-26443 shows the push-to-stage control assumed by RFC-002 failing open: when the hydrator sync source changes before the external promoter has moved fresh manifests, auto-sync deploys whatever the stage branch last held — old manifests reach the cluster with no dry commit corresponding to the deployed state, breaking RFC-002's core auditability promise that 'every deployed change must have a corresponding dry commit.' The deployment happened under the controller's identity with no promotion decision on record for it.

The PRD's Security Considerations assert 'no additional roles or privileges are needed... no impact on the security aspects,' but T-28511 documents that the reverse deletion order it introduces produces an infinite delete/re-create loop when a child is deleted manually, and the incident runbook in note-2 now requires operators to hand-flip ApplicationSets to `AllAtOnce` before any manual child deletion. A feature declared security-neutral has in fact created a standing manual operational control whose omission causes uncontrolled resource churn — an exposure the PRD's risk section ('No immediate Risks to consider') does not acknowledge.

T-27833's proposal — split resource handling so namespace creation runs under the Argo CD control-plane SA while sync runs under the impersonated SA with `kind: Namespace` removed — presupposes per-resource identity selection, which RFC-001 explicitly forecloses: 'the service account to be used for impersonation is determined on a per Application level rather than on per resource level.' The ticket's requested permission boundary (users unable to smuggle namespace manifests past `clusterResourceWhitelist` via git) cannot be built on the impersonation design as specified; neither document acknowledges the other.

The published roadmap commits that ordered or automated deletion of ApplicationSet children 'will not be implemented' and that teardown 'remains a manual operator action', while the PRD proposes shipping exactly that capability as the deletionOrder field (AllAtOnce/Reverse) inside ApplicationSetStrategy. Both commitments cannot hold; shipping the PRD puts the organization in breach of its published roadmap statement, and note-2 records that the disagreement was spotted but assigned no owner.

RFC-002 makes git the organization's system of record for change auditing (Use case 1: 'strong requirements around change auditing') and has the commit server push hydrated commits whose README and hydrator.metadata carry the dry commit's human commitAuthor, while T-28239 states those machine-generated commits are pushed unsigned today. The result is machine-generated writes entering the audit record attributed to a human author with no cryptographic or procedural means to distinguish the machine act from the human act; until commitserver.sign.hydrated.commits exists and is enabled, authorship of the hydrated history can only be assumed, not proven.

RFC-001 answers its accountability question by asserting that Kubernetes audit trail events 'capture both the actual user and the impersonating user' so it is 'possible to track who executed the commands.' T-28695 shows the diff path ignores destinationServiceAccounts and runs as the shared cluster credential (User 'argocd'), and T-26271 shows CI diffs running as system:serviceaccount:argocd:argocd-server. Acts recorded in the audit trail therefore do not consistently map to the per-Application identity model RFC-001 relies on for attribution: some operations by the same feature are logged under a shared service identity that cannot be tied to a responsible tenant.

RFC-001's Goals state the impersonation feature 'can be enabled/disabled only at the system level. Once enabled/disabled, it is applicable to all Argo CD Applications', but note-1 records a platform-call decision that the rollout 'goes behind a per-project flag, not fleet-wide' and calls it 'a real decision, not a maybe.' The governance decision grants a permission granularity the approved design document says does not exist; one of the two records must change or the recorded decision is unimplementable as written.

Note-1 and ticket T-26271 describe the same failure without the ticket saying so: the missing-permissions CI diff error was root-caused on the platform call (with impersonation on, diff runs as the destination service account lacking patch on cluster-scoped resources), but the ticket still records the reporter chasing the broad cluster Secret credential. The organization's authoritative record for this defect lives only in an informal meeting dump; the system-of-record ticket carries the wrong theory of cause.

The PRD's Risks and Mitigations section states 'No immediate Risks to consider' and its Security Considerations assert 'no impact on the security aspects', but T-28511 documents a reproduced production-class failure of the very mechanism the PRD specifies: an ApplicationSet configured with rollingSync plus the reverse deletion strategy enters an infinite delete/re-create loop when a child Application is stuck Progressing, and note-2 records it reproducing in staging with an incident-runbook mitigation (switch to AllAtOnce before manual child deletion). The PRD's risk record and the incident record cannot both stand.

RFC-002's push-to-stage mode explicitly delegates movement of changes to the deployment branch to 'some external system' (the promotion integration point), and note-1 records that this external system is 'still the shell script, nobody owns it.' Responsibility for what actually deploys has moved from Argo CD to an unowned artifact with no named holder, and T-26443 shows the concrete failure mode: in push-to-stage mode, auto-sync deploys whatever stale manifests the branch last held when the promoter has not yet acted. If a stale deployment causes harm, no document names the accountable owner of the promotion step.

Every ticket in the corpus carries the provenance line 'verbatim base; see PROVENANCE.md for edits', but no PROVENANCE.md exists in the corpus. The edit record that would distinguish the verbatim upstream text from local modifications is absent, so for every ticket the organization relies on, which statements are original third-party content and which are internal edits can only be assumed, not proven — a defect in the provenance of the records themselves.

Licensed-review recommendation: the combination of a single cluster-wide GPG signing key held in a namespace Secret (T-28239) and a GitHub App private key granting repository-write access held as a Kubernetes secret (RFC-002's 'Push access' section) means automated components will produce signed, attributed records in the audit history on behalf of the organization and its developers. Whether such machine-signed commits satisfy the organization's electronic-signature, records-retention, and change-audit obligations, and who is legally accountable when the shared key signs a bad change, is a question for licensed counsel in the organization's operating jurisdiction; this review does not answer it.

The strategy roadmap commits, under 'First class support for ApplicationSet resources', that ordered or automated deletion of ApplicationSet children 'will not be implemented' and teardown remains a manual one-Application-at-a-time operator action, while the PRD's stated Goals are to ship exactly that automation as the deletionOrder field (AllAtOnce/Reverse) in ApplicationSetStrategy. Both commitments cannot hold; the incident review note already flags the disagreement as needing an owner, so the call is currently unowned.

The PRD's Risks and Mitigations section states 'No immediate Risks to consider', but field evidence contradicts it: T-28511 reproduces an infinite delete/recreate loop when an ApplicationSet configures rollingSync with the reverse deletion strategy and a child is stuck Progressing (the wait-for-full-deletion semantics the PRD specifies for Reverse never completes), and the incident runbook's standing mitigation is to switch deletion to AllAtOnce before any manual child deletion. The PRD's Reverse goal is built on an assumption the incident record has already falsified.

RFC-001's Goals state the impersonation feature 'can be enabled/disabled only at the system level. Once enabled/disabled, it is applicable to all Argo CD Applications', but the platform sync call decided rollout 'goes behind a per-project flag, not fleet-wide' — recorded as 'a real decision, not a maybe'. The approved spec offers no per-project enablement mechanism, so the rollout decision cannot be executed against the spec as written.

T-26271 (CLI diff via argocd-server, in-cluster) and T-28695 (application-controller reconcile diff on external clusters) are the same underlying gap: RFC-001's Implementation Details only fix the sync path (Application Controller sync.go setting Impersonate config on SyncContext), so Server-Side Diff's dry-run patch still runs as the cluster Secret credential rather than the AppProject's destinationServiceAccounts. Note-1 records the root cause for T-26271 and asks that it be noted on the ticket; T-28695 independently rediscovers it and shows the consequence (unbounded patch RBAC growth, Synced/Unknown flapping).

Impersonation cannot be flipped on for any project until 'the diff story is fixed' per the platform sync decision, yet no ticket or spec owns the diff-path fix: RFC-001's component list contains no diff/comparison work, and T-28695's only remedy today is the documented opt-out ServerSideDiff=false. The gating condition for the entire impersonation rollout therefore has no planned deliverable behind it.

T-27833's proposal depends on splitting resource handling between the control plane SA (namespace creation via CreateNamespace=true) and the impersonated SA per resource kind, but RFC-001 explicitly resolves in its Open Questions that the impersonation service account is determined 'on a per Application level rather than on per resource level'. The security boundary the reporter needs (users escaping pod-security labels by committing Namespace resources) cannot be closed by the impersonation feature as specified, yet the ticket is relying on it.

RFC-002 declares 'Implementing a change promotion system' a Non-Goal and delegates push-to-stage promotion to 'some external system', but the organization is already depending on that out-of-scope piece: T-26443 shows auto-sync deploying stale manifests specifically in push-to-stage mode when the external promoter has not yet moved fresh manifests, and note-1 records that the stage-branch promoter is 'still the shell script, nobody owns it' — parked, not staffed. The hydrator's staging mode ships with its correctness dependent on an unowned script.

T-27327 states rollback is 'one of the first questions we get when onboarding new users' to the source hydrator rollout, but note-1 deprioritizes that same History & Rollback ticket to next quarter while the hydrator pilot continues (T-27949 confirms a repository is actively piloting the hydrator). The rollout promise (onboarding users now) and the resourcing decision (rollback next quarter) collide: pilot users are onboarded onto a deployment path with no rollback story.

T-27949 and note-2 describe the same interaction from two sides without citing each other's conclusion: the ticket reports that on the hydrator pilot repo 'every hydration cycle lands a fresh commit on the hydrated branch... picked up as a source change', and the incident review confirmed 'each hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave', ruling that hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until a debounce exists — a restriction the review explicitly asked to be carried on T-27949 and which the ticket does not yet carry.

T-28927 proposes promoting Progressive Sync to Stable ('tested and validated with various use cases') on the basis that key execution issues are addressed, but the corpus's own evidence undermines the success measure: T-27846 states that 'getting a wide-eye view of progressive sync is difficult' and the metrics needed to observe step timing, wave triggers, and stalled syncs do not yet exist, while T-27949 (rollout reports complete with children OutOfSync) and T-28511 (delete/recreate loop) are open defects in exactly the RollingSync mechanics being declared mature. The data to know Stable criteria are met does not exist yet.

RFC-002's Opinions section rules out 'Multiple sources referenced in the same application' and unpinned Helm chart dependencies as incompatible with deterministic hydration, recommending the umbrella-chart approach instead; T-24417 reports that this exact recommendation ('switching to helm dependencies') breaks the ApplicationSet workflow for controlling chart versions across environments and asks for a Chart field on DrySource. The field request and the RFC's determinism opinion pull the DrySource contract in opposite directions, and no one owns reconciling them.

T-24578 (Source Hydrator for ApplicationSets, motivated by controlling destroy order across ApplicationSets) and the PRD's deletionOrder proposal are addressing the same user need — ordered deprovisioning of ApplicationSet-generated Applications — through two different mechanisms (hydrated app-of-apps with sync waves vs. a deletionOrder field on ApplicationSetStrategy), with neither document referencing the other. Whichever ships first partially obsoletes the other's motivation, and the strategy doc currently promises neither will ship.

The strategy roadmap commits that deletion of ApplicationSet-generated Applications is explicitly out of scope ('ordered or automated deletion of ApplicationSet children will not be implemented... teardown remains a manual operator action'), while the PRD's stated goal is exactly that: a deletionOrder field with a Reverse strategy that deletes applications in the reverse order of the rollingSync steps. Both commitments cannot hold; note-2 records the disagreement was noticed but left without an owner.

The PRD's Risks and Mitigations section asserts 'No immediate Risks to consider', but T-28511 documents a production-shaped failure of the same mechanism: with rollingSync plus a deletion-order strategy, a child Application stuck in Progressing makes the 'wait for one Application to be fully deleted' step never complete and the controller loops deleting/re-creating resources. Note-2 confirms the loop reproduced in staging specifically with the reverse deletion order, so the PRD's risk claim is already falsified by the organization's own incident record.

T-28927 defines the scope to promote Progressive Sync to Stable while the observability that would validate maturity is still an open request: T-27846 asks for the basic metrics (time to trigger, time per step, refreshes caused by the ApplicationSet, 'why is my sync not starting'), and T-27949 shows the cost of the gap in practice — its rollout-reported-complete-while-OutOfSync failure produced no evidence because 'controller logs were at warn level, so no relevant progressive-sync transition logs were emitted'. Stable promotion depends on measurements nobody is recording, and no document links the promotion issue to the metrics ticket.

Note-2's interim rule that hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync 'until there's a debounce' and T-27949's aside that the pilot repo sees every hydration commit picked up as a source change describe the same mechanism: each hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave. The only counter that would make this restriction verifiable or removable — 'how much Application refresh were caused by the ApplicationSet' — is item 3 of the open metrics request T-27846, so today the wave-restart behavior is unobservable in production and the restriction's exit condition cannot be measured.

T-26271's reporter blames the broad cluster Secret and expects the 'ArgoCD Application Controller service account' to produce the diff, but note-1 records the actual root cause decided on the platform call: with the sync impersonation flag on, the diff runs as the destination service account, which lacks patch on cluster-scoped resources — precisely the decoupling RFC-001 introduces via destinationServiceAccounts and application.sync.impersonation.enabled. The root cause was never written onto the ticket, so the ticket's stated expected behavior points at the wrong component.

RFC-001 commits that the impersonation feature 'can be enabled/disabled only at the system level. Once enabled/disabled, it is applicable to all Argo CD Applications', while note-1 records the rollout decision that 'it goes behind a per-project flag, not fleet-wide... that's a real decision, not a maybe.' The decided rollout unit (per-project) does not exist in the designed control surface (a single argocd-cm / environment-variable toggle), so the rollout plan cannot be executed against the spec as written.

Note-1 gates impersonation rollout on 'the diff story is fixed', but that gate has no measurable exit criterion, and T-28695 shows the diff gap is structural, not a one-off: Server-Side Diff runs as the cluster Secret credential rather than the destinationServiceAccounts identity, RBAC has no dry-run verb, and each new chart forces another unbounded patch grant (five rounds recorded). The only numbers in the corpus that would move if this fired fleet-wide are T-28695's own ComparisonError / Synced-to-Unknown rotation, which no ticket or note proposes to track; the gate can therefore stay open indefinitely or be declared closed without evidence.

T-26443's stale-sync bug ('we only observe this when the hydrator runs in push-to-stage mode; the external promoter has not yet moved the fresh manifests') and note-1's parked flag that 'our stage-branch promoter is still the shell script, nobody owns it' are the same exposure: RFC-002's push-to-stage mode explicitly 'relies on some external system to move changes to the deployment branch', and that unowned shell script is the system whose lag lets auto-sync deploy whatever the stage branch last held. No document ties the promoter's ownership gap to the bug it produces.

Note-1 deprioritizes the hydrator rollback ticket T-27327 to next quarter and moves the dev pair to the deletion loop, while the hydrator pilot continues on live repos (T-27949 is piloting the source hydrator). T-27327 itself records that rollback is 'one of the first questions we get when onboarding new users' and that hydrator-enabled apps cannot use the existing History & Rollback tab — so during the deferral window the pilot's only recovery path is manual git surgery on the sync branch, an exposure no pilot ticket carries and whose incidence (rollbacks needed on hydrated repos) nobody is counting.

T-24578's ask for controlled destroy ordering of ApplicationSet-generated Applications during cluster deprovisioning is the demand signal for the PRD's deletionOrder feature, yet neither cites the other: the ticket says users are forced into app-of-apps workarounds because 'ApplicationSets don't support DAG-based Application destroy ordering', which is exactly the dependency-ordered deletion the PRD's Reverse strategy provides, and it bears on the PRD's open question of whether a custom order 'is needed' (the ticket wants cross-ApplicationSet DAG ordering, which Reverse alone does not cover).

T-28695's workaround evidence — 'Measured cost: zero' for disabling Server-Side Diff — is a baseline drawn only from ~20 monitoring charts on that reporter's external clusters, while T-26271 shows a different population (in-cluster CLI diff in CI against cert-manager) hitting the same error string with different scoping. If the organization generalizes the 'zero cost' number when deciding the diff story that gates impersonation rollout (note-1), it is reusing a baseline measured on one workload shape for a fleet-wide decision, with no before/after diff-accuracy measurement requested anywhere in the corpus.

T-26271's CI diff failure ('is attempting to grant RBAC permissions not currently held') is explained by RFC-001's design decision to apply impersonation only to the Application sync operation (setting Impersonate config on the SyncContext in sync.go): with application.sync.impersonation.enabled turned on, server-side diff dry-runs execute under the narrower destination service account, which is exactly the root cause recorded at the platform sync call and never written back onto the ticket, leaving the reporter chasing the broad cluster Secret credential.

T-28695's application-controller symptom (sync honors destinationServiceAccounts, Server-Side Diff runs as the cluster Secret credential and demands unbounded patch RBAC on external clusters) is the same design gap: RFC-001's Implementation Details scope impersonation to the sync operation and GitOps Engine kubectl commands only, and nowhere address the diff path, so 'diff runs as a different identity than sync' is a direct consequence of the proposal's boundary, not a regression.

T-28511's delete/recreate infinite loop is explained by the PRD's Reverse deletionOrder semantics: the PRD specifies Reverse 'waits for one application to be fully deleted before moving onto the next', and the ticket observes precisely that a resource stuck in Progressing means the wait never completes and the wave restarts from the top; yet the PRD's Risks and Mitigations section says 'No immediate Risks to consider' with this symptom already filed against the mechanism, and the incident review's AllAtOnce-before-manual-delete runbook rule exists only in raw notes.

The strategy roadmap commits that deletion of ApplicationSet-generated Applications is 'explicitly out of scope for rollout orchestration' and that teardown 'remains a manual operator action, performed one Application at a time', while the PRD proposes shipping a deletionOrder field (AllAtOnce/Reverse) that automates ordered deletion of ApplicationSet children; both commitments cannot hold, and note-2 records the disagreement was noticed but left without an owner.

T-27949's hydrator-pilot aggravation (every hydration cycle lands a fresh commit on the hydrated branch and each is picked up as a source change, restarting the RollingSync wave) is explained by RFC-002's design that each dry commit produces a new hydrated commit per environment targetBranch which the application controller then syncs; the incident review's interim rule that hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until a debounce exists lives only in note-2 and is not carried on the pilot ticket or acknowledged in the RFC.

T-26443's symptom of auto-sync deploying stale manifests when the syncSource changes occurs specifically in RFC-002's push-to-stage mode, where the design explicitly 'relies on some external system to move changes to the deployment branch'; note-1 records that this external system is still an unowned shell script promoter, tying the reported staleness directly to the decision to delegate freshness to an out-of-scope promoter.

T-27327's rollback proposal (git checkout of an old rendered revision committed directly to the sync branch, bypassing the staging branch) cannot hold together with RFC-002's stated opinion and goal 4 that 'every deployed change must have a corresponding dry commit' and that change lineage is fully represented as a series of dry commit hashes: a checkout-based rollback commit on the sync branch has no originating dry commit, breaking the promotion rules RFC-002 says the dry-hash lineage exists to enable.

T-27833's proposed remedy (split which resources the Argo CD control-plane SA handles versus the impersonated SA, so namespaces can be created by the control plane but denied to the tenant SA) collides with a decision RFC-001 has already made: the impersonation service account is determined 'on a per Application level rather than on per resource level', so the ticket's per-resource split is precluded by the design it proposes to use, and neither document acknowledges the other.

Note-1 records the decision that impersonation ships behind a per-project flag and 'nobody flips it on a project until the diff story is fixed', but RFC-001 specifies the feature 'can be enabled/disabled only at the system level' via applicationcontroller.enable.impersonation, applicable to all Applications once enabled; the agreed rollout control does not exist in the design, so any enablement exposes every project at once to the diff-identity failures documented in T-28695.

T-24578's request for Source Hydrator support on ApplicationSets to control destroy order across a cluster's Applications and the PRD's deletionOrder for ProgressiveSync are two uncoordinated solutions to the same underlying need (ordered teardown of ApplicationSet-generated Applications); neither document cites the other, so the DAG-based cross-ApplicationSet ordering the ticket asks for is not represented in the PRD's single-ApplicationSet Reverse strategy.

proposals.change: Record that the hydrator history & rollback work is deprioritized to next quarter, and the dev pair moves to the progressive sync deletion loop instead.
proposals.citedLine: hydrator rollback work (the history & rollback ticket, T-27327) is deprioritized to next quarter. dev pair moves to the progressive sync deletion loop instead. ticket should say so.

proposals.change: Record that the delete/recreate loop reproduced in staging with the reverse deletion order, and the interim mitigation: the incident runbook says switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce deletion before deleting any child app by hand, until the controller fix lands.
proposals.citedLine: the delete/recreate loop (T-28511) reproduced in staging with the reverse deletion order. mitigation for now: incident runbook says switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce deletion before deleting any child app by hand. that's the operational rule until the controller fix lands — worth remembering as a standing practice.

proposals.change: Record the confirmed finding that each hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave, and the interim restriction from the incident review: hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until a debounce exists.

deltas.citedLine: impersonation rollout: we decided it goes behind a per-project flag, not fleet-wide. nobody flips it on a project until the diff story is fixed. that's a real decision, not a maybe.

deltas.body: Standing operational rule until the controller fix lands: switch an ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce deletion before manually deleting any child app.
deltas.citedLine: the delete/recreate loop (T-28511) reproduced in staging with the reverse deletion order. mitigation for now: incident runbook says switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce deletion before deleting any child app by hand. that's the operational rule until the controller fix lands — worth remembering as a standing practice.
